name: Heat Haze
basis: live refractive displacement rising with time (how)

lumenary.blurb: Warm air rising bends the light that passes through it. The picture shimmers upward from the heat, tinted a little warmer where it is hottest. The cursor is a flame.

why: Warm air is thinner than cool air, and thinner air bends light a little less. Over a hot road the air is a shifting mix of slightly different densities, so the rays of light that cross it are bent from moment to moment and the view wobbles. The ripples rise because the warm air itself rises.
how: Use the Gladstone-Dale relation n − 1 = Kρ: the refractive index depends on density, and density depends on temperature, ρ ∝ 1/T at constant pressure.
Build a displacement field from fractal noise stretched vertically (horizontal frequency 1.3 times the vertical 0.45, in units of ripple size).
Scroll the noise upward as time passes, so the ripples rise.
Read the picture at each pixel’s displaced position, stronger near the heat source (the bottom, the centre, or everywhere).
Shift the red and blue channels slightly apart for colour fringes, and add a warm tint where it is hottest.
history: In the seventeenth century Robert Hooke noticed that hot air rising from a candle bends light, and in 1864 August Toepler built the schlieren method to photograph such invisible flows. Mirages on deserts and roads are the same effect on a bigger scale. Stars twinkle for a similar reason, and astronomers call the blur the seeing.
uses: Heat shimmer over roads, engines and fires in film and games
Schlieren photography of airflow and shock waves
terms: A number that says how much a material slows and bends light.
An image bent by layers of air at different temperatures.
A method of photographing changes in air density.
paragraphs: Air bends light. How much depends on its density, through the Gladstone-Dale relation n − 1 = Kρ, and density depends on temperature, ρ ∝ 1/T at constant pressure. So warm air rising from the ground is a swirling mix of slightly different refractive indices, and the rays that pass through it are deflected a little differently from moment to moment. That is the shimmer over a hot road. The program displaces each pixel’s lookup of the picture by a vector built from fractal noise stretched in the vertical direction (the horizontal frequency is 1.3 times the vertical one’s 0.45, in units of the ripple size), and the noise scrolls upward as time goes on, so the ripples rise. The displacement is up to 3.2% of the width at full strength, a little less sideways than up and down, with a slight net lift.

A heat weight w from 0 to 1 says how hot each place is. It rises from the bottom as smoothstep(0.1, 1, y/H)^1.3 for heat from the ground, is a broad Gaussian blob for heat from the middle, or is 0.8 everywhere. The pointer adds a Gaussian flame around itself that eases in at 4 per second and out at 2 per second. Red and blue light are bent by slightly different amounts (dispersion), and the program reads the three channels with the displacement scaled by 1 − s, 1 and 1 + s, which gives colour fringes at edges; s is 0.9 × the colour fringes slider. The warm tint adds red and yellow in proportion to the local displacement. The field is computed on a lattice of 6 px cells at half size and interpolated bilinearly.

equations.note: Why warm air bends light: hot air is thinner, so its refractive index is lower.
Displacement of the lookup: A is 0.032 × strength × width, w the heat weight, λ the ripple frequency, τ the time.
Each colour channel is looked up with its own share of the displacement.

presets.text: Heat from everywhere shakes the whole picture.
Fine, quick ripples look like a desert road.
Strong colour fringes and a warm tint make a fierce furnace.
